figures.caption: Figure 1 :  Observed BDI-II scores by visit and treatment arm, comparing treatment as usual (TAU) with  Beating the Blues  (BtheB), on the bounded scale from 0 to 63 and shown as boxplots with overlaid individual observed values. The dashed horizontal lines mark the lower and upper bounds of the score.

Figure 2 :  Observed proportion of missing BDI-II values by visit and treatment arm, comparing treatment as usual (TAU) with  Beating the Blues  (BtheB). Proportions use the retained analysis set as the denominator within each arm: 45 subjects for TAU and 52 for BtheB. Missingness increases substantially over follow-up in both arms.

Figure 3 :  Illustration of the thresholded latent Gaussian construction for a representative setting with mass at the lower bound,  ( μ , σ ) = ( − 1.1 , 1.0 ) \left(\mu,\sigma\right)=\left(-1.1,1.0\right) , which induces approximately  Pr ⁡ ( Y i ​ t = L i ) = 0.09 \Pr\left(Y_{it}=L_{i}\right)=0.09  and  Pr ⁡ ( Y i ​ t = U i ) = 0.00 \Pr\left(Y_{it}=U_{i}\right)=0.00 . The left panel shows the latent Gaussian density with threshold locations  a i a_{i}  and  b i b_{i} . The right panel shows the corresponding distribution on the observed scale, obtained from 1,000,000 simulated draws under the thresholded observation rule, with the red vertical line indicating the point mass at the lower boundary. The interior histogram is scaled so that its area plus the probabilities at the two bounds equals one.
Table 1:  Simulation Study 3: population treatment effect inference at the final visit when the imputation and generating truth rules match.

Table 2 :  Comparison using leave-one-subject-out prediction of common score intervals. Higher ELPD indicates better predictive performance. Differences are relative to the continuous bounded model; their SEs account for pairing by subject.

Figure 4 :  Application to the  BtheB  data: visit-specific treatment arm differences in mean BDI-II under the MAR, WJ2R(0.50), J2R, and CR sensitivity rules. Points show estimates pooled using Rubin’s rules after fitting an MMRM to each of 50 posterior predictive completed datasets under each rule. Error bars show the corresponding 95% intervals. Negative values favor  Beating the Blues , since lower BDI-II indicates fewer depressive symptoms.

Figure 5 :  Posterior predictive profiles of mean BDI-II and the probability of a score of exactly zero under MAR, WJ2R(0.50), J2R, and CR for BtheB, with TAU under MAR as the reference. Points show posterior means and bars show pointwise 95% intervals for the completed cohort summaries, with observed outcomes held fixed. All 4,000 post-warmup draws were used. Profiles are offset horizontally for readability. Intervals collapse to points at month 2 because all outcomes at that visit were observed.

Web Figure 1 :  Observed mean BDI-II by visit and treatment arm, comparing treatment as usual (TAU) with  Beating the Blues  (BtheB). Error bars show approximate pointwise 95% confidence intervals computed using normal theory from the available cases at each visit.

Web Figure 2 :  Observed proportion of BDI-II scores at the lower bound by visit and treatment arm, comparing treatment as usual (TAU) with  Beating the Blues  (BtheB). Proportions are calculated among subjects with an observed score at each visit within each treatment arm. Values of exactly zero become more prominent later in follow-up.

Web Figure 3 :  Subject trajectories of BDI-II by treatment arm, comparing treatment as usual (TAU) with  Beating the Blues  (BtheB). The trajectories illustrate heterogeneity across subjects, a general downward trend over time, occasional values of exactly zero, and incomplete follow-up for many subjects before the final visit. Open black circles indicate the last observed BDI-II value for subjects whose final available assessment occurred before the last scheduled visit.
